questions.q: Épernay, home of Moët & Chandon and the Avenue de Champagne, stands on the banks of which river?
questions.exp: The Marne flows west past Épernay and gives its name to the Vallée de la Marne, where Meunier leads in the west and Pinot Noir around Aÿ and Mareuil. The Court pairs it with the Grande Montagne de Reims, the wooded plateau to the north whose slopes hold nine of the seventeen Grand Cru villages; Reims itself stands on the Vesle.

questions.q: What does a Champagne house usually add to the liqueur de tirage so that the deposit slides cleanly down into the neck at riddling?
questions.exp: The liqueur de tirage is wine with about 24 grams of sugar a litre, selected yeast, a yeast nutrient and a riddling aid such as bentonite or alginate, which makes the spent yeast fall as a heavy, compact deposit. The liqueur d'expédition, added after disgorging, is wine with sugar or concentrated grape must, and its sugar sets the style from Brut Nature to Doux.

questions.q: By the Court's figures, which grape covers the largest share of the Champagne vineyard, about 38 per cent?
questions.exp: The Court gives the plantings as 38 per cent Pinot Noir, 32 per cent Meunier and 30 per cent Chardonnay, so the two black grapes cover about seven tenths of the vineyard. Pinot Blanc is one of the minor permitted varieties with Pinot Gris, Arbane and Petit Meslier, and the specification of 2025 added Chardonnay rose.

questions.q: What is the Comité Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne that the Court names in its classification row?
opts: The joint body of growers and houses
The club of the great houses
questions.exp: The Comité Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne, now styled the Comité Champagne, brings the growers and the houses together to manage the appellation's shared business: harvest yields, the reserve, research, promotion and the defence of the name. The national appellation authority is the INAO; the Échelle des Crus, the other term in the Court's row, ranked the villages as Grand Cru or Premier Cru.

questions.q: Which collective term does the Court use for Champagne's great historic houses, such as Krug, Roederer and Taittinger?
questions.exp: Grandes Marques, the great brands, is the name for the large historic houses, taken from a syndicate of houses that existed until the 1990s; it has no legal standing today. The Court asks a Certified candidate to match the Grandes Marques to their prestige cuvées and to know three producers outside them and three growers.

questions.q: A guest orders La Grande Dame from the prestige page of the list. Which house made it?
questions.exp: La Grande Dame, a Pinot Noir dominant vintage cuvée, is named for the widow Clicquot, who ran the house from 1805 and is credited with the riddling table. Other pairings the Court expects: Dom Pérignon from Moët & Chandon, Cristal from Louis Roederer and Comtes de Champagne from Taittinger.

questions.q: Which of these producers is a grower, a récoltant-manipulant making Champagne only from its own vines?
questions.exp: Larmandier-Bernier is a grower at Vertus in the Côte des Blancs, making biodynamic Chardonnay with low dosage, and its labels carry the code RM. Taittinger, Veuve Clicquot and Moët & Chandon are négociant-manipulant houses (NM) that buy much of their fruit; the Court asks for three growers beside the Grandes Marques.
